Schadenfreude is the feeling of pleasure, satisfaction, or even quiet delight that you get when something bad happens to someone else. Not just any pleasure — specifically the pleasure that comes from their misfortune. The misfortune is the source of your good feeling.

Notice that this is a very specific emotion. You're not happy despite someone else's bad luck. You're happy because of it. That "because of" is the entire soul of this word.
What makes it unique

Most emotions have straightforward names in English — joy, anger, sadness, envy. But schadenfreude describes something so precise and so socially uncomfortable that English never developed its own word for it, and had to borrow this one from German. The fact that a whole word exists for it tells you something important: this is not a rare or exotic feeling. It is deeply, universally human. Almost everyone has felt it at some point, even if they'd never admit it out loud.
The unspoken ingredient: a reason to not feel sorry

Schadenfreude almost never appears randomly. It tends to show up when the person suffering is someone you have a reason — real or imagined — to not feel fully sorry for. This could be because you dislike them, because you feel they're arrogant, because you think they deserved what happened, or simply because they were in a higher or more fortunate position than you and their fall feels like the universe balancing itself out.

This is crucial. If a complete stranger you had no feelings about slipped and got seriously hurt, most people would feel concern, not schadenfreude. But if the person who had been mocking you all week tripped in front of everyone? That flicker of hidden satisfaction — that's schadenfreude.
Everyday examples

Here are some situations where you might feel schadenfreude:

Your classmate barely studies, brags about it constantly, and then fails a test you both took. You feel a small, warm glow of satisfaction. You didn't want to fail — you're glad you passed — but there's an extra layer of pleasure that comes specifically from their failure.

A rude driver cuts you off aggressively in traffic. Two minutes later, you pass them pulled over on the side of the road with a police officer. You feel a burst of something deeply satisfying, something that makes you smile to yourself.

A celebrity who is famous for being arrogant and dismissive gets publicly embarrassed at a big event. Even people who don't know them personally feel a ripple of amusement and satisfaction.

An office bully, who has been making everyone's life difficult for months, finally gets a sharp reprimand from the boss in front of the whole team. Their colleagues struggle to keep straight faces.

In every one of these cases, the pleasure you feel is not accidental — it is specifically triggered by the misfortune of the other person. That is schadenfreude.
It comes in different intensities

Schadenfreude is not one-size-fits-all. It exists on a spectrum.

At its lightest, it's a brief, harmless chuckle — like finding it funny when someone confidently walks into a glass door. No real harm done, no real animosity, just a moment of amusement at someone else's embarrassing mishap. This kind of schadenfreude is so mild that most people don't even feel guilty about it.

In the middle of the spectrum, it's the quiet satisfaction you feel when someone who acted superior, dishonest, or unkind gets their comeuppance. This is where schadenfreude gets most interesting psychologically, because it often feels tied to justice — like the world got something right.

At its strongest and darkest, schadenfreude becomes more troubling — when someone takes genuine, deep pleasure in serious suffering, especially of someone who didn't truly deserve it. Most people, if honest, would feel uncomfortable about this level.
The psychology behind it

Schadenfreude has real roots in how humans relate to one another socially. A big part of it comes from social comparison — the way we unconsciously measure ourselves against others. When someone who was doing better than us suddenly stumbles, the gap between us shrinks. We feel momentarily elevated, even if our actual circumstances haven't changed at all.

Another driver is envy. Research in psychology consistently shows that schadenfreude is strongest when directed at people we envy. If someone has something we want — status, talent, beauty, success — and then publicly fails, the envy we were carrying gets replaced by a fleeting sense of relief or satisfaction. The person no longer feels untouchably superior.

A third driver is a sense of justice or fairness. Humans have a powerful in-built sense of fairness. When someone acts badly — is cruel, dishonest, arrogant, or unfair — and then suffers consequences, it doesn't just feel satisfying. It feels correct. Schadenfreude in this case is essentially your brain saying "the world made sense today."
What schadenfreude is NOT

It is not sadism. Sadism means getting pleasure from deliberately causing someone else pain. Schadenfreude is passive — you didn't do anything to make the bad thing happen. You simply feel pleased when it does.

It is not gloating. Gloating is what you do — it's the outward act of rubbing someone's nose in their failure. Schadenfreude is what you feel internally. You can feel schadenfreude completely privately, in silence, without a single word or expression. Many people do exactly that, because the emotion carries social stigma.

It is not indifference. If you simply didn't care that something bad happened to someone, that's neutrality. Schadenfreude is the opposite of indifference — it is an active positive feeling sparked by the negative event.
The moral dimension

Most people feel a slight pang of guilt alongside schadenfreude, as if they have just caught themselves thinking something they shouldn't. This is because the emotion conflicts with a deeply held social value — that we should feel sympathy when others suffer. Feeling pleased instead feels wrong.

But here is an important and honest thing to understand: feeling schadenfreude does not make you a bad person. It makes you human. It is an automatic emotional response, not a deliberate moral choice. The difference between a good person and a cruel one is not whether they ever feel schadenfreude — almost everyone does — but what they do with it. A person of good character notices the feeling, perhaps smiles privately, and then moves on without acting on it or magnifying it. They don't pile on, they don't gloat, and they don't seek out others' suffering as a form of entertainment.
How to use it in a sentence

"He tried to look sympathetic when his rival's business failed, but his schadenfreude was written all over his face."

"There's a certain guilty schadenfreude in watching a pompous public figure get knocked down a peg."

"She felt a flash of schadenfreude when the colleague who had dismissed her ideas was now asking for her help."

Note that it is frequently used with words like guilty, quiet, secret, or undeniable — because the feeling is so often something people experience but feel they shouldn't. These qualifiers have practically become part of the word's personality in English.
The one-sentence summary
Schadenfreude is the pleasure you feel — often guiltily, almost always privately — when misfortune strikes someone else, especially someone you resent, envy, or feel has deserved it.
SHAHD-n-froy-duh
